en: The Ten Forms of Drama.
[Chapter One] Homage to that Gaṇeśa, whose trunk acts as a water-lily.
The deep roar of the intoxicated peacock during its dance.
Through the imitation of the ten forms, practitioners of aesthetic emotion (bhāvaka) are intoxicated;
homage to that Viṣṇu, the all-knowing, and to Bharata.
Only occasionally, out of compassion, does Sarasvatī bestow her domain upon some learned man; another person then praises that rare individual by whose means he attains eloquence.
Having repeatedly extracted the essence from all the Vedas, Viriñci composed this Nāṭyaveda; its practical application was performed by the sage Bharata, the Tāṇḍava dance by Nīlakaṇṭha,
and the Lāsya dance by Śarvāṇī at every step— who else is able to describe its further characteristics?
However, I shall briefly state the definition of dramas with some degree of systematic arrangement.
In that which is scattered [over many texts], a confusion of mind arises for those of dull intellect;
therefore, its meaning is being set forth directly by means of those very words, in a concise form. (Dharmapada-daśottara 1.5)

Even that person of small intellect who, like [those who rely on] the Itihāsas and so forth, says that the fruit in poetic works— which overflow with bliss— is merely proficiency in expression, speaks correctly.
Homage to him who turns his back on the sweet.

Drama (*nāṭya*) is an imitation of states; it is called "form" (*rūpa*) because it is visible. It is a "dramatic representation" (*rūpaka*) due to superimposition, and it rests upon the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) in ten ways.

The drama (nāṭaka), along with the play-with-plot (prakaraṇa), the monologue (bhāṇa), the farce (prahasana), the heroic drama (ḍima), the mixed drama (vyāyoga), the combined drama (samavakāra), the dramatic scene (vīthī), the interlude (aṅka), and the deer-play (hāmṛga). // DhDaś_1.8 //
Dance (nṛtya) is based on emotion, while choreographed dance (nṛtta) is based on rhythm and tempo;
the former is the dramatic representation of the meaning of words, while the latter is the regional style. DhDaś_1.9 //
Each of those two types is further divided into two— namely, the sweet (*madhura*) and the exuberant (*uddhata*)—
and takes the form of *lāsya* and *tāṇḍava*, thereby serving as an aid to drama and other literary forms.
The subject matter (vastu), the hero (netā), and the sentiment (rasa) are the differentiators; and the subject matter is of two kinds.
Among these, they know the primary to be the central plot (adhikārika) and the secondary to be the incidental (prāsaṅgika).

Authority is the ownership of the fruit, and authority is the master of that [fruit]. That which is to be accomplished by it, pervading it, is the conduct pertaining to authority (ādhikārika). DhDaś 1.12.

That in which the welfare of others occurs incidentally as a consequence of one's own welfare is called *sānubandha* (with a sequel) or *patākā* (the banner); while *prakarī* (the episode) pertains to a specific portion [of the plot].
That for which the welfare of others is incidental, and one’s own welfare follows as a consequence;
that which possesses a continuous connection and is characterized by an equal arrangement.

That [plot] is also threefold according to the distinction between the well-known (*prakhyāta*), the invented (*utpādya*), and the mixed (*miśra*); each of these is again threefold. The well-known is derived from sources such as history (*itihāsa*); the invented is fashioned by the poet; and the mixed arises from a combination of those two. Furthermore, there is a division based on the characters, such as celestial beings, mortals, and so forth. (Dhvanyāloka 1.15)
The task is the threefold aim (trivarga), which is pure and connected to both the singular and the manifold. Its cause is briefly indicated as the seed, which expands in many ways.
When there is an interruption in the intermediate matter, a "drop" (bindu) serves as the cause for non-interruption.

The five types of plot-essences (arthaprakṛti) are proclaimed as follows: those known as the seed (bīja), the drop (bindu), the banner (patākā), the episode (prakarī), and the purpose (kārya). DhDaś_1.17 //
For those who seek the fruit of an undertaking that has been begun, there are five stages of the task:
initiation, effort, hope for attainment, certainty of attainment, and the arrival of the fruit. (Dharmasaṃgraha 1.18)
The mere onset of eagerness is for the sake of attaining a greater fruit;
however, when that is not attained, exertion is an activity characterized by extreme haste. (Dharmasamuccaya 1.19)
Through the absence of fear regarding [the lack of] means or [the possibility of] misfortune, there arises the hope for attainment and the possibility of attainment.
Because of the absence of misfortune, attainment is certain; this is the well-ascertained "attainment of certainty.
The "union with the fruit" is the perfection of the complete fruit, as previously described.
The five fundamental subjects, endowed with five states, give rise respectively to the five junctures beginning with the introduction (mukha). DhDaś 1.21.
Sandhi is the connection between two parts when there is a single underlying purpose;
it consists of the Mukha, Pratimukha, Garbha, Avamarśa, and Upasaṃhṛti. (Dhvanyāloka 1.22)
The "mouth" is the origination from the seed, which gives rise to various meanings and flavors;
its twelve limbs arise through the connection with the commencement of that seed. (Dharmadhātustava 1.23)
Introduction, preparation, conclusion, enticement, application, attainment, resolution, arrangement, and cultivation;
then the disclosure and differentiation—these are the names according to their meaning, as well as their defining characteristics. (Dharmasaṃgraha 1.24)
The sowing of seeds is the introduction; its abundance is the elaboration;
its completion is the conclusion; and from the narration of qualities comes the enticement. (Dharmasaṃgraha 1.25)
The thorough deliberation of meanings is reasoning; attainment is the arrival at happiness;
the arrival of the seed is meditative concentration; and the application is that which produces pleasure and pain. (Dharmapada 1.26)
The manifestation of a previously cultivated and extraordinary state of possession is "unfolding" (udbheda), which is the breaking open of what was hidden.

"Instrumentality" (karaṇa) is the commencement of the primary practice; this is considered "differentiation" (bheda). "Encouragement" (protsāhanā) is also recognized as a form of differentiation. (Dharmakīrti’s *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya* 1.27)
The "Subsequent Opening" (pratimukha) should be like the emergence of that [plot] while it is both visible and invisible;
following from the development of the "Bindu" and "Preliminary Effort," its constituent parts (aṅgas) are thirteen.
Vilāsa, parisarpa, vidhūta, śamana, narma, narmadyuti, pragayaṇa, nirodha, and paryupāsana. (Dharmasaṃgraha 1.29)
The "vajra" is the introduction; the "flower" is also called the withdrawal of color.

"Grace" (vilāsa) is the pursuit of pleasure; "gliding" (parisarpa) is the following after what has been seen and lost. "Shaking off" (vidhūta) is the absence of desire; its cessation is tranquility (śama). (Dharmasaṃgraha 1.30)
Parihāsa is jesting; narma is cheerfulness, and the radiance arising from it is considered *dyuti*;
*uttarā-vāk* is a retort; *pragayaṇa* is the obstruction of what is beneficial, which is *nirodhana*.
Service, conciliation, the "flower," speech that is distinguished,
the "introduction" which employs skillful means, the "thunderbolt" which is direct and harsh,
the "approaching of the four castes," and the "withdrawal of castes"— these are recognized as the [eight] ornaments. (Dharmapada 1.32)
The "embryo" (garbha) is the repeated searching for a seed that was seen and then lost;
it consists of twelve factors. It may or may not be the "banner" (patākā), as there is the possibility of its attainment.
False accusation, the paths, the sequence in the illustration of form, compendium, inference, and likewise the *toṭaka* and *adhivala*. (Dharmapada-daśottara 1.34)
Agitation, confusion, and interruption are defined as its characteristics;
"the non-existent" refers to deception, while the "path" is the proclamation of the true meaning. (Dharmasamuccaya 1.35)

Form is like discursive thought; speech accompanied by self-exaltation is called "illustration"; sequence is the attainment of what is being reflected upon; and others say it is the knowledge of dispositions. (Dharmasaṅgraha 1.36)

Conciliation is the utterance of conciliatory words; conjecture is inference from signs; a superior strategy is a well-aimed intention; and *saṃrabdha* is speech that is forceful or mocking. (Dharmasaṃgraha 1.37)
Agitation,
fear, apprehension, terror, and confusion arise;
because it pierces the seed of the embryo, this is proclaimed as *ākṣepa* (the sudden interruption).

Where one should touch [the plot] through anger, or through calamity, or through seduction—that *avamarśa* (crisis), which has the purpose of manifesting the seed of the plot within the womb, is the collection of constituent parts (*aṅga*). (Dharmakīrtidāsa’s Daśarūpaka 1.39)

In that regard, there are thirteen [types of speech]: censure, quarreling, flight, agitation, power, brilliance, attachment, deception, resolve, opposition, incitement, wavering, and taking up. (Dharmapada 1.40)
The proclamation of faults is *pravyāhāra*; *sampheṭa* is speech uttered in anger;
*vidrava* is execution, imprisonment, and the like; *drava* is the disparagement of one's teacher. (Dharmapada 1.41)
The pacification of conflict, power, intimidation, causing alarm, radiance, the glorification of the Guru, the relevant context, deception, and humiliation. (Dharmapada 1.42)
Resolve is the expression of one's own power; opposition is the defiance of those who are provoked.
Application is that which reveals the future through successful consultation.
Boasting is wavering; undertaking is the grasping of the task. (Dharmasamuccaya 1.43)

When the elements such as the opening (mukha) and others, which possess their respective seeds and were scattered according to their proper places, are brought together toward a single purpose, that indeed is the Conclusion (nirvahaṇa).

The fourteen [sections] are: the connection (sandhi), the awakening (vibodha), the composition (grathana), the determination (nirṇaya), the discourse (paribhāṣaṇa), favor (prasāda), joy (ānanda), the occasion (samaya), the deed (kṛti), the speech (bhāṣā), the embrace (upagūhana), the prior state (pūrvabhāva), the conclusion (upasaṃhāra), and the eulogy (praśasti). DhDaś 1.45.
The connection, the arrival at the seed, awakening, the seeking of the effect,
the tying together, its introduction, and the narration of what was experienced— these constitute the conclusion.
Paribhāṣā is mutual conversation; prasāda is service;
ānanda is the attainment of what is desired; and samaya is the departure from suffering. (Dharmasaṃgraha 1.47)
The accomplishment of the goal, the pacification [of obstacles], the attainment of honor and so forth, and the discourse;

the vision of the task, the attainment of the marvelous, and the concealment of previous states; the attainment of the boon, the conclusion of the poem, and the eulogy consisting of the proclamation of auspiciousness. (Dharmapada 1.48)

The composition of the desired subject matter, the concealment of what should be hidden, its revelation, passion for the performance, the marvelous nature of the narrative, and the lack of deficiency in the plot—these are the qualities [of a drama]. (Dharmakīrti’s Daśarūpaka 1.49)
A twofold division must be made of every single thing:
some may be merely expressible, while others are visible or audible.
In that [work], a detailed expansion of the plot that is flavorless or inappropriate should not be indicated;
rather, what is to be seen must be a continuous flow of sweet and noble sentiments and aesthetic moods.
One should present what is to be indicated by means of five types of thematic introductions:
the *viṣkambha*, the *cūlikā*, the *aṅkāsyā*, the *aṅkāvatāra*, and the *praveśaka*. (Dharmakīrti’s Daśarūpaka 1.52)
The *viṣkambha* (interlude) indicates portions of the story already narrated and those yet to be told; it summarizes the meaning and is performed by middle-ranking characters.

It may be enacted by one or several characters, and is classified as pure (*śuddha*) or mixed (*saṅkīrṇa*) according to whether the characters are low or middle-ranking. (Dharmakīrti’s Daśarūpaka 1.53)
In the same way, an entrance performed by a low-ranking character, indicated by an unaccented (anudātta) utterance at the end of two acts, serves as a pointer to the remaining plot.
The *cūlikā* is the indication of the plot's meaning by means of characters situated behind the inner curtain;
the *aṅkāsyaka* is the indication of the plot of a broken act by means of characters at the end of an act. (Dharmakīrtidāsa’s Daśarūpaka 1.55)
The entry into an act occurs at the end of the preceding act through the non-separation of one act from another;
by these means one should indicate what is to be indicated, and one should demonstrate the visible action through the acts.

With regard to the rules of dramatic performance (nāṭyadharma), this subject matter (vastu) is further considered to be threefold: that which is to be heard by all, that which is restricted to certain individuals, and that which is not to be heard at all. (DhDaś 1.57)
That which is audible to all is considered *prakāśa* (open); that which is not audible is considered *svagata* (aside).
Another two-fold category is called *nāṭyadharma* (theatrical convention), consisting of *janāntika* (whispering to one person) and *apavārita* (speaking so as not to be overheard by others).

When one converses with others while excluding others by means of the *tripatākā* hand gesture, that mutual address in the presence of people is called *janāntika*. When something is told in secret to another by turning away from others, it is called *apavārita*.
"What do you say? and so forth—when one speaks thus without a recipient, even though it is unheard by another, that speech is as if it were directed toward empty space. (Dharmapada 1.60)

Having thus contemplated all these various categories of entities without exception— including the *Rāmāyaṇa* and other works, as well as the *Bṛhatkathā*— one should subsequently compose [the work], in accordance with the hero and the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
He tells a wonderful tale with an elaborate array of appropriate and charming words.
[Chapter 2] The leader is disciplined, sweet-natured, generous, capable, and pleasant of speech.
He is beloved by the world, pure in speech, of noble lineage, steadfast, and youthful.

Endowed with intelligence, enthusiasm, mindfulness, wisdom, skill, and mental composure; heroic, firm, radiant, possessing the eye of the scriptures, and righteous—this [heroic style] is fourfold through its varieties: the playful (lalita), the calm (śānta), the noble (udātta), and the haughty (uddhata).
Free from anxiety, graceful and composed, devoted to the arts, happy, and gentle;
yet possessing ordinary qualities, such as the twice-born and others, is the *dhīraśānta* (the calm and steadfast). DhDaś_2.3 //
The Mahāsattva is exceedingly profound, patient, and free from boastfulness;
he is steadfast, with his ego concealed, noble-minded, and firm in his vows.
Abounding in pride and envy, devoted to deceit and guile, he is haughty and arrogant, unstable, fierce, and boastful. (Dharmapada 2.5)
The *dakṣiṇa* (courteous), the *śaṭha* (deceitful), and the *dhṛṣṭa* (bold) are each captivated by another woman while facing his former mistress.
The *dakṣiṇa* is affectionate toward her [present mistress], while the *śaṭha* performs secret acts of displeasure against her.
The *dhṛṣṭa* openly displays physical deformities; however, the *anukūla* (compliant) man has only one mistress. (Dharmakīrti’s Daśarūpaka 2.6)
But the hero of the banner is another, the discerning *pīṭhamarda*;
he is his devoted follower, slightly inferior to him in virtues. (Dharmapada-daśottara 2.7)
The *viṭa* is one type of man-about-town, while the *vidūṣaka* is another who provides comic relief;
the enemy is one who is greedy, arrogant, stubborn, a doer of evil, and addicted to vices.
Beauty, grace, sweetness, profundity, fortitude, splendor,
charm, and magnanimity— these eight are the human qualities born of the quality of goodness (sattva).
In the state of *dhṛṇā* (pride), there is superiority; in *spardhā* (rivalry), there is valor and skill;
in *śobhā* (grace), the gait is full of composure and the gaze is steady; and in *vilāsa* (playfulness), speech is measured.
Gentleness is a transformation that remains sweet even during great agitation;
profundity is that by whose power no transformation is perceived.
Steadfastness is the lack of wavering from one's resolve even in the face of a multitude of obstacles;
brilliance is the inability to endure insults even when life itself is at stake. (Dharmapada 2.12)
The state of possessing the gestures and movements of the erotic sentiment is natural grace;
gentleness consists in giving life through pleasant speech, while generosity is the noble act of kindly reception.
The heroine is of three types: one's own, another's, and a common woman.
One's own heroine is endowed with modesty, sincerity, and other such virtues; she is further classified as inexperienced, intermediate, or mature. (Dharmadāsa’s Daśakumāracarita 2.14)
The innocent girl, desirous through her fresh youth, is resistant in love yet gentle in anger;
with the youthful god of love beginning to rise within her, she is capable of enduring sexual union until she reaches the height of delusion.
A steadfast woman annoys her lover with sarcastic and crooked speech; a middling woman does so with tears and feigned anger; but an unsteady woman, out of rage, torments him with harsh words.

Blinded by youth and intoxicated by passion, the bold woman seemed to melt with joy against the body of her beloved, becoming unconscious even at the commencement of sexual union. (Dharmakīrti’s Daśakumāracarita 2.17)
In love-making, the *madhyā* (middle-aged woman) is full of affectation and respect, while in anger she is the opposite of firm;
having rebuked him, she should strike him. The *madhyā-adhirā* (middle-aged woman who is firm) should speak to him in that same manner.
The *amugdhā* (the non-ignorant woman) is said to be of twelve types, divided into two: the *jyeṣṭhā* (elder) and the *kaniṣṭhā* (younger). // DhDaś_2.18 //
A maiden married to another man, or one wedded by someone other than her father, may never [be approached] according to the school of Aṅgiras;
however, out of a desire for the maiden's affection, she may engage in union with him through mutual bodily contact.

A common woman is a courtesan who is endowed with artistic skill, boldness, and cunning; she is one who knows how to conceal her lustful pleasures, is independent, and is full of pride toward eunuchs. (Dharmapada 2.20)
Like a passionate woman, she entices the wealthy; like a mother, she banishes the destitute. Yet, unlike a passionate woman, she does not laugh in jest, for she has no recourse to gods or kings.
These women have eight stages, beginning with "she whose husband is under her own control" (svādhīnapatikā) and so forth;
she whose lover is nearby and dependent on her is the "delighted one" (hṛṣṭā), known as svādhīnabhartṛkā.
The woman preparing for her tryst adorns herself with joy at the thought that her beloved will arrive;
but when he delays, though he is not unfaithful, she becomes distracted, her mind filled with the longing of separation.
When [the transgression] is known and revealed through attachment to another, she is stained by the bitterness of broken jealousy;
when shaken by the resentment of being separated by a quarrel, she is joined with the pain of lingering regret. (Dharmapada-daśottara 2.24)

One who has been deceived after making a rendezvous, one who is deeply insulted because the lover did not arrive at the appointed time, and one whose beloved is away on business in a distant land—such a woman, afflicted by love, may go to meet her lover or cause him to come to her; she is called an *abhisārikā*. (Dharmakośa 2.25)

The six [types of grief] are characterized by anxiety, sighing, exhaustion, tears, discoloration, and languor; the last two are joined with the first two, while the [two] breasts are characterized by radiance and great joy.

Female messengers should be a maidservant, a female friend, a female artisan, the daughter of a paternal aunt, a neighbor, a female ascetic, or a female craftsman; they should be one's own kin or endowed with the qualities of a leader or a friend. (Dharmasamuccaya 2.27)
In youth, there are twenty ornaments born of the nature of women;
among these, three—bhāva, hāva, and helā—are born of the body.
Beauty, loveliness, brilliance, sweetness, eloquence, generosity, and steadfastness—these seven qualities are produced without effort. (Dharmapada 2.29)

Līlā (sportiveness), vilāsa (graceful movement), vicchitti (elegance), vibhrama (confusion), kilakiñcita (mixed emotion), moṭṭāyita (affected indifference), kuṭṭamita (feigned anger), bibboka (haughtiness), lalita (charm), and vihṛta (coquetry)— these ten are to be known as the emotions born of natural disposition.
From the quality of *sattva*, which is of an unchanging nature, there arises "being" (*bhāva*), which is the first modification;
therein, *hāvaka* is the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), while *hāva* consists of modifications of the eyes and eyebrows. (Dharmakīrti’s Daśanāmasaṃgraha 2.31)

That very playfulness, clearly indicative of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), serves as the ornament for her limbs through the beauty of her form, enjoyments, and youth. (Dharmakīrti’s *Daśakumāracarita*, 2.32)
That very luster, cast with the shadow of the god of love, is known as *kānti* (loveliness).
*Mādhurya* (sweetness) is the quality of being smooth, while *dīpti* (brilliance) is the expansion of *kānti*.
Fearlessness, boldness, magnanimity, constant humility, freedom from fickleness, fortitude, and a mental disposition free from boastfulness; DhDaś_2.34 //
*Līlā* is the imitation of a beloved through sweet movements of the limbs;
*vilāsa*, however, is a momentary distinction in the actions of the limbs and so forth. (Dharmakīrti’s Daśarūpa 2.35)
Even a slight arrangement of ornaments produces an enhancement of beauty;
however, confusion regarding the timing and the reversal of the proper places for ornaments results from haste. (Dharmakīrti’s Daśakumāracarita 2.36)
*Kilakiñcita* is the mingling of anger, tears, joy, fear, and so forth;
*moṭṭāyita*, however, is the contemplation of the lover's state of being during pleasant conversations and the like. (Dharmapada-daśottara 2.37)

With joy within, she should display a feigned agitation when her hair or lip is grasped; and even when addressed by one she desires, she should show disdain through pride and arrogance. (Dharmapada-daśottara 2.38)
A graceful arrangement of delicate limbs and smoothness constitutes the *lalita* (graceful) style;
however, that which one does not speak when the time is right due to shame is indeed the *vihṛta* (hesitant) style.
The minister, himself, or both together, are his friends in deliberating on affairs;
the others are merely "playful" (lalita) ministers, for all successes depend upon the minister.

The officiating priests and the family priest [are concerned] with dharma; the ascetics and those who discourse on Brahman [are concerned] with austerity; friends, princes, and forest-dwellers [are concerned] with punishment; and the vassals and soldiers [are concerned] with the army. (Dharmapada 2.41)
In the inner apartments, there were eunuchs, Kirātas, the mute, the dwarfs,
Mlecchas, Ābhīras, Śakas, and others, each employed for their respective duties.
All [characters] possess a threefold nature according to whether they are superior, middling, or inferior;
and based on the gradation of the aforementioned qualities, they are classified as excellent and so forth.
In this manner, the hero, along with his retinue, should be fashioned in drama.

The *vṛtti* (mode of performance), which consists of their respective functions, is fourfold therein; among them, the *kaiśikī* is gentle, characterized by movement, dance, dalliance, and so forth, as well as amorous gestures such as jesting (*narma*), *taisphiñja*, *tatsphoṭa*, and *tadgaibha*, and it possesses four constituent parts (*caturaṅgikā*).
Playful wit, jesting, and the act of conciliating a beloved—these three forms of *narma* (jest) are fashioned through humor, erotic passion, and fear respectively. (Dharmadāsa-daśakumāracarita 2.45)
The erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is also threefold through self-reproach, enjoyment, and pride;
the pure (*śuddha*), the limb (*aṅga*), and fear (*bhaya*) are each twofold; and everything is accompanied by laughter (*sahāsya*). Thus, the playful jest (*narma*) is said to be eighteenfold.
In a new union, *narmasphiñja* is a pleasant beginning that ends in fear;
*narmasphoṭa*, however, is the disclosure of internal states indicated by small tastes through fragments.
The Kaiśikī [vṛtti] here consists of these elements: concealed glances, conduct, jesting, and purposeful speech, accompanied by limbs that are smiling or not smiling. (Dharmakīrti’s Daśarūpaka 2.48)
That [drama] is free from sorrow, characterized by the Sāttvata style, and possesses the qualities of courage, generosity, compassion, and straightforwardness;
within it, there are the *saṃlāpa*, *utthāpaka*, *sāṅghātya*, and *parivartaka* [sections]. (Dharmakīrti-daśottara 2.49)
The *saṃlāpaka* is one whose speech is profound and who converses with others on the essence of various states;
the *utthāpaka*, however, is one who at the outset rouses the opponent for battle.
The *sāṅghātya* [plot] arises from the combined power of spells, meaning, fate, and so forth; the *saṅghabhedana* [plot] from the division of a group;
and the *parivartaka* [plot] from performing another task than the one that had been commenced. (Dharmakīrti’s Daśarūpaka 2.51)
Through these elements, this [Sāttvatī] is fourfold; furthermore, Ārabhaṭī consists of activities such as illusions, magic, battle, rage, and agitation.
Saṅkṣiptikā occurs through [the use of] gestures, while Sampheṭa consists of the emergence and falling away of dramatic subjects.
Condensation is the concise arrangement of subject matter through the application of artistic skill;
it consists of the departure of the previous narrator and the adoption of another narrator.

*Saṃpheṭa*, however, is a clash between two who are enraged and agitated. The production of a thing through the employment of illusions and the like is intended as *vastūtthāpana*. *Avapāta*, moreover, consists of exits, entries, terrors, and flight.
Through these components, this function of meaning is fourfold;
beyond that is the fourth, Bhāratī, which must also be mentioned in the definition of drama.
Reciting "Kaiśikī, Sāttvatī, Ārthī, and Ārabhaṭī," the followers of Udbhaṭa proclaim a fifth style (vṛtti). DhDaś_2.56.

The Kauśikī style is used in the erotic sentiment; the Sāttvatī and Ārabhaṭī styles, moreover, in the heroic; and the Bhāratī style is employed everywhere in the furious, the odious, and all other sentiments.
The modes of conduct should consist of the local dialects, activities, and dress;
having understood these from the world itself, one should employ them as is appropriate.
However, water for the feet (pādya) that has been consecrated may be offered to men of self-restraint who are not of low birth,
to those bearing religious marks (liṅgin), to the Great Goddess (Mahādevī), and occasionally to the daughter of a minister and to a courtesan.

For women, however, [the dialect] is generally Prākṛta; among the lowest, such as the Śūrasenīs, it is Paiśāca; and likewise for Piśācas, extremely low castes, and others, it is Māgadhī. (Dharmapada-daśottara 2.60)
Whatever region a lowly vessel belongs to, in that same region his speech should be;
furthermore, for the sake of the task at hand, the use of a different dialect by those who are otherwise superior and so forth may be permitted.

The Blessed Ones should be addressed with honorifics; likewise those who possess the marks of learned ones, celestial sages, and ascetics; as well as Brahmins, ministers, elders, and noble men; and actors and actresses may address one another during the performance of a play.

The venerable one is addressed as "charioteer" by the driver; disciples, sons, and younger brothers address him as "venerable one"; and even a father, though worthy of honor, is addressed as "child" by those who have properly received their names.

A master is addressed as "bhāva" by a subordinate, and as "sūtrī" by a fellow official; he is addressed as "mārṣa" by his peers, as "deva" or "svāmī" by servants, as "nṛpati" by commoners, and as "bhaṭṭa" by the lowest.

Women are to be addressed according to their husbands, whether they be superior, middling, or inferior; a female servant may be addressed as "hale," a maidservant as "hañje," and likewise a courtesan as "ajjukā."

She is honored as "Mother" by those who have followed her from her days as a procuress, or as "Old Lady" by the common folk; yet by the Vidūṣaka, you are addressed as "Queen" or "Maid. (Dharmasamuccaya 2.66)
Who is capable of describing in their entirety the gestures, qualities, utterances, and mental states— each distinguished by the ten stages of the leader (the actor),
were it not Bharata?
Or rather, he who is not a god with the crescent moon upon his crest. [Chapter 3] Furthermore,
because they are the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of others, and because they possess an abundance of essence (*rasa*).
And because it possesses all the defining characteristics, it is called a *nāṭaka* first.
Having first performed the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga) and once the stage-manager (sūtradhāra) has exited,
another actor shall enter and present the poetic work (kāvyam) in the same manner.

In that [plot], whether divine or human, being of such a nature, he may indicate—either one of those two mixed together—the plot-matter (*vastu*), the seed (*bīja*), the opening (*mukha*), or even the character (*pātra*). (Dharmakīrti-daśottara 3.3)
Having gratified the audience with sweet verses that indicate the themes of the poem,
one should adopt a particular season and resort to the *bhāratī* style of composition.

Bhāratī is the verbal activity, consisting primarily of Sanskrit, which rests upon the actor; it is characterized by various divisions such as the prologue (prarocanā), the benediction (vīthī), and the introductory scene (āmukha).
In that context, "making [the audience] attentive" (*unmukhīkaraṇa*) consists of praise and incitement (*prarocanā*).
The *vīthī* and the *prahasana* will also be discussed in their own relevant sections; however, because they are constituent parts of the *āvyamukha*, they are mentioned here once again. (DhDaś 3.6)
When the Sūtradhāra speaks to the Naṭī, or to a Mārṣa, or to a Vidūṣaka, introducing his own business by means of striking speech, that is the Āmukha (Prologue). (Dharmakīrtidāsa’s Daśarūpaka 3.7)

In that regard, there may be the prologue (prastāvanā), which consists of the introductory scene (kathodghāta) and the commencement of the action (pravṛttaka), as well as the excellence of performance (prayogātiśaya); furthermore, there are thirteen elements of the vīthī. DhDaś_3.8 //
When an actor enters after having grasped a sentence or a meaning that is similar to his own conduct, that is the "Commencement of the Story" (kathodghāta), which is of two kinds.
*Pravṛttaka* is that in which the entry of a character occurs simultaneously with the conclusion of the preceding [act].
Where the entry of a character occurs through the director’s performance by means of an introductory suggestion such as "This is he," this is considered *prayogātiśaya*.

The thirteen [types of] frivolous speech (*mṛdvāṇī*) are: *udghātyaka*, *avalagita*, *prapañca*, *trigata*, *chala*, *vākkeli*, *adhivala*, *gaṇḍa*, *avasyandita*, *nālīka*, *asatpralāpa*, *vyāhāra*, and *mṛdvāṇī*. (Dharmasaṃgraha 3.11)
When there is a mutual dialogue consisting either of a series of words with hidden meanings or a sequence of questions and answers, that is called the two-fold *udghātyaka*.
Where, through a convergence in one place, another effect is accomplished;
or where, while something else is under discussion, another [effect] occurs—that is *āvalagita*, which is twofold. (Dharmakīrti-daśottara 3.13)
Mutual praise that is unreal is considered to be "prapañca" (prolixity) which causes laughter;
however, here "trigata" (the triple movement) is the application of multiple meanings based on similarity of sound,
and it is desired in this context as the dialogue among the triad of actors and others during the *pūrvaraṅga* (preliminary rite).

Deceit (*chala*) consists of enticement and deception through words that are either pleasant or unpleasant; it may involve withdrawing from a conversation or responding two or three times. (Dharmasaṃgraha 3.15)
The *adhivala* occurs when one speaks with excessive words in response to another out of rivalry;
the *gaṇḍa* is that which is uttered suddenly as a different meaning than what was intended by the context. (Dharmakīrti’s Daśakumāracarita 3.16)

When that which was spoken with a specific intent is explained otherwise, it is indeed *avasyandita*; when it contains hidden meaning and is accompanied by irony, it is *nālikā* or *prahelikā*. (Dhvanyāloka 3.17)
That which consists mostly of irrelevant talk is idle chatter (*asat-pralāpa*), each subsequent type being more so;
speech uttered for some other purpose, words that provoke laughter or dance, and where faults are treated as virtues and virtues as faults—that indeed is frivolity (*mṛdu*). (Dharmasaṃgraha 3.18)

Having cast aside either the subject matter or the vessel with one of these [methods], the holder of the Sūtra should depart at the end of the introduction; thereafter, he should elaborate upon the main body of the work.
Endowed with qualities that inspire confidence, firm and noble, possessed of majesty,
desirous of fame, great in energy, and a protector of the three Vedas, he is a lord of the earth.

Where the hero is a divine royal sage (rājarṣi) from a renowned lineage, that should be designated as "Renowned" (prakhyāta); the primary action (vṛtta) therein is the one pertaining to the central plot. (Dharmakīrtidāsa’s Daśarūpaka 3.21)
Whatever in that [work] is unsuitable for the hero or for the aesthetic flavor (rasa), being contradictory, should be abandoned or otherwise modified. (DhDaś 3.22)
Having thus determined the beginning and the end, and having divided that into five parts,
one should further subdivide each fragment and the portions designated as joints.
Furthermore, it is said that there should be sixty-four such constituent parts (*aṅga*).

Even in the *patākā* type of drama, which lacks one or more of the junctures (*sandhi*), one should place the constituent parts as they occur, including the *prakārī*, even if it is without a formal juncture. (DhDaś 3.24)
At the beginning, one should employ either a *viṣkambhaka* (interlude) or an act (*aṅka*), according to the requirements of the plot;
when there is a remainder of the narrative that must be shown—having omitted the tedious expansion of the subject matter—one should then employ a *viṣkambhaka*. (Dharmakīrtidāsa’s Daśarūpaka 3.25)
But when a subject matter proceeds from its very root with aesthetic flavor,
then at the very beginning there should be an *aṅka* based on the introduction (*āmukha*) and the *ākṣepa*.
An act (aṅka) is one in which the characters are witnessed directly, which is preceded by the pervasion of the *bindu*,
and which serves as a locus for the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) through the arrangement of various types of plot elements.

The nourishment of the dominant emotion (aṅgin) must be accomplished through the determinants (vibhāva), the consequents (anubhāva), the permanent emotions (sthāyin), and the transitory emotions (vyabhicārin), by means of their being grasped and released. DhDaś 3.28.

One should not, by means of excessive sentiment, lead an object to a state of extreme remoteness, nor should one obscure the sentiment with the characteristics of objects or poetic ornaments. (Dharmadāsa-daśakumāracarita 3.29)

One single rasa must be accepted as the primary sentiment—either the heroic (vīra) or the erotic (śṛṅgāra)—while all other rasas should serve as its subordinate elements; at the conclusion, one should employ the marvelous (adbhuta).

A long journey, execution, battle, the ruin of one's kingdom or country and so forth, imprisonment, eating, bathing, sexual intercourse, and the application of unguents—[these are to be avoided]. (Dharmasamuccaya 3.31)
One should not point out the seizing of clothes and other such acts as being perceptible;
nor should one ever abandon the killing of those who have committed an offense, even if it is necessary.
An act (*aṅka*) consists of a single day’s events, shares a single purpose, and has its protagonist situated nearby;
it involves three or four characters, and at its conclusion, there is their exit. (Dharmakīrti-daśarūpaka 3.33)
In this [drama], the *patākāsthānaka*s, the *bindu*, and the *bīja* should be employed at the end; likewise, the *aṅkas* should be composed, preceded by entries and other such elements.
This [drama] is inferior with five *aṅkas*, while the supreme *nāṭaka* has ten *aṅkas*.
Now, in a *prakaraṇa*, having established a plot based on worldly life, one should make a single minister, brahmin, or merchant the hero. (Dharmakīrti’s Daśarūpa 3.35)

The wise and serene [drama] contains adversity, is devoted to the goals of Dharma, Artha, and Kāma, and like other dramas, it includes junctures (*sandhi*), interludes (*praveśaka*), the aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*), and so forth. DhDaś 3.36.
The heroine, however, is of two kinds: the wife of a noble family and the courtesan;
in some cases there is only one of the noble-born type, in some cases both, and in others [only the courtesan]. (Dhvanyāloka 3.37)
There are women of noble birth, those from within [the household], and courtesans from outside; there is no transgression regarding these two [categories].
Through them, the subject matter is divided into three parts, crowded with rogues. (Dharmakośa 3.38)
A *nāṭikā* is also observed here [in this work] for the purpose of excluding other mixed forms.

In that genre, the plot is derived from a *prakaraṇa* or a *nāṭaka*; the hero is a renowned king, characterized as *dhīralalita* (calm and playful); and the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is the predominant rasa, possessing its defining marks. (Dhvanyāloka 3.39)
If it is intended that there be divisions such as those with four acts primarily featuring women,
then there would be infinite forms due to the distinctions of one, two, three, or more acts, and so forth.
In that case, the queen should be the eldest, bold, born of a royal lineage, profound, and proud; through great difficulty, the union with the leader occurs under her influence.
Such a heroine is innocent, divine, and exceedingly enchanting;
she is close at hand through her connection with the inner apartments and others, by means of hearing and sight.
As the passion of the leader for her progresses through its nine stages,
he proceeds therein apprehensive of the Goddess’s alarm,
like a *nāṭikā* (short drama) characterized by the four *kaiśikī* limbs and distinct acts. (Dharmakīrti’s Daśakumāracarita 3.43)
A *bhāṇa*, however, is where a single clever and learned wit describes the conduct of rogues—either his own experience or that of another. (Dharmasaṃgraha 3.44)
One should perform the dialogue of address and response through speeches directed at empty space;
one should indicate the heroic and erotic sentiments through praises of valor and charm.

For the most part, the *bhāratī* style is employed; the plot consists of a single act, contains the *mukha* and *nirvahaṇa* junctures with their constituent parts, and includes all ten *lāsyāṅga* elements. (Dhvanyāloka 3.46)
The Geya consists of a verse standing, a Pādya of one seated, a Puṣpagaṇḍikā, a Pracchedaka, a Trigūḍha, and that called Saindhava which has two hidden [verses]. (Dharmapada 3.47)
The Utta-mottamaka and the Uktapratyukta—these indeed constitute the tenfold classification of the limbs of Lāsya. (Dharmapada 3.48)

In the same way, the comic (prahasana) is of three kinds, according to its being pure, deformed, or mixed. It is crowded with heretics, Brahmins, and the like, as well as servants, maidservants, and lechers;
it consists of actions performed through gestures and speech, and is pure, accompanied by humorous words. (Dharmakirti’s Daśarūpaka 3.49)

With the attire of lustful men and the like, including eunuchs, chamberlains, and ascetics, the street should be made varied through such mixture and crowded with rogues; however, the sixfold sentiment, primarily the comic (hāsya), should be predominantly employed. (Dharmakīrtidāsa’s Daśarūpaka 3.50)
In the *ḍima*, the subject matter should be well-known; the styles (*vṛtti*) are present except for the *kaiśikī*;
the protagonists are gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, mahoragas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and so forth—sixteen in number—and they are exceedingly haughty. (Dharmadāsa’s Daśarūpaka 3.51)

It is endowed with six radiant aesthetic sentiments (rasas), excluding the comic and the erotic, and with activities such as illusions, sorcery, battle, wrath, and agitation. (Dharmapada-daśottara 3.52)

When eclipses of the moon and sun occur, and when the dominant sentiment (rasa) is the Furious (raudra), the *ḍima* is defined as having four acts, four junctures (sandhis), and no *nirvimarśa*. (DhDaś 3.53)
The *vyāyoga* has a well-known plot and relies on exalted characters;
it is devoid of the *garbha* and *vimarśa* junctures, and its sentiments (*rasas*) should be as radiant as those of a *ḍima*.
A *vyāyoga* is a single-act play performed in a single day, involving many men, such as the battle fought by the son of Jamadagni against those who were not women. (Dharmakīrti’s Daśarūpaka 3.55)
In the *samavakāra* as well, the prologue (*āmukha*) is like that of the *nāṭaka* and other forms;
its subject matter is the well-known conflict between gods and asuras, and the junctures (*sandhi*) are devoid of deliberation.
The styles (vṛtti) are those of the soft Kaiśikī; the leaders are gods and dānavas;
twelve [characters] are renowned as noble (udātta), and their fruits are distinct for each.
All [these] possess the flavor of many heroes (bahuvīrarasa), just as in the churning of the ocean;
they consist of three marks (aṅka), three deceptions (tripaṭa), three amorous elements (triśṛṅgāra), and three types of flight (trividrava). (Dharmapada-daśakarma 3.58)
The first act, containing two double-meanings, should consist of twelve *nālikās*;
the last two [acts] should each consist of four *nālikās*, and a *nālikā* is equal to two *ghaṭikās*.
Three types of deception may arise from the nature of things, fate, or human agency:
namely, the siege of a city, battle, and the panic caused by wind, fire, and so forth. (Dharmapada 3.60)

In this [genre], erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) is pursued through the aims of dharma, artha, and kāma; it does not contain *vindu* or *praveśaka* sections, and one should employ the components of the *vīthī* as they occur, just as in a farce (*prahasana*).

The *vīthī*, however, follows the *kaiśikī* style; its junctures (*saṃdhi*) and constituent parts (*aṅga*) are like those of the *bhāṇa*. The sentiment (*rasa*) to be indicated is the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), though it may also touch upon other sentiments.
The *vīthī* should be composed in this manner, employing the introductory elements such as the *udghātyaka* and others, and performed by two or one actor. (Dharmakīrti-daśottara 3.63)
In the *utsṛṣṭikāṅka*, one should expand upon the well-known narrative through the intellect;
the sentiment (*rasa*) is the pathetic (*karuṇa*), the permanent emotion (*sthāyin*) is [sorrow], and the protagonists are ordinary men.

Employing the ornaments of speech, the functions of composition, and the poetic meters, one should wage a battle of words with lamentations like those of women; in this manner, victory and defeat are achieved.
In the *Miśramoha* deer-play, there are four acts and three junctures;
the hero and the antagonist are respectively human and divine, according to the rules. (Dharmakīrtidāsa’s *Daśarūpaka* 3.66)
In the case of fame, the last two [styles], the bold (*dhīra*) and the haughty (*uddhata*), are characterized by perversion and improper conduct;
for example, when one desires to abduct a celestial woman against her will through theft and other such means.
One should display to him here and there some semblance of the erotic sentiment;
having brought him to the height of fury, one should dissuade him from battle through various pretexts.
One should never carry out the execution of that great-souled being who has been brought to the point of death.
Having reflected thus, having examined the path of the definitions of the ten types of drama, and having contemplated the subject matter of the works of great poets,
one should compose a literary work with ease, adorned with poetic figures.
With words that are noble and sweet, and clearly composed in a slow tempo;
[Chapter 4] with the determinants (*vibhāva*), the consequents (*anubhāva*), the involuntary states (*sāttvika*), and the transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*).
The stable emotion (sthāyibhāva), when brought to a state of being relished, is known as aesthetic flavor (rasa).
In that context, the determinant (vibhāva) nourishes the emotion by being known;
it is twofold, distinguished as the objective basis (ālambana) and the excitant (uddīpana). DhDaś_4.2 //
The *anubhāva* (consequent) is a transformation consisting in the indication of the *bhāva* (inner state);
the establishment of these two, as cause and effect, occurs through conventional usage.
The cultivation of those states consists in the mental cultivation of states such as pleasure and pain;
other states, though they are manifestations of feeling, are distinct as the *sāttvika* [emotions],
because they arise from *sattva* alone, and that is what constitutes the cultivation of those states.

Stupefaction, fainting, horripilation, perspiration, change of color, trembling, tears, and loss of voice—these are the eight [external signs]. Among these, stupefaction is the state of the limbs becoming motionless; fainting is the loss of consciousness; the remaining ones have clearly manifest characteristics. (Dharmapada 4.5)

Moving toward their objects with particular intensity, the transitory emotions (vyabhicārin) rise and submerge within the permanent emotion (sthāyin), like waves in the ocean. (Dharmakīrti’s Daśāvatāracarita 4.6)
Disgust, languor, apprehension, fatigue, fortitude, dullness, joy, dejection, ferocity, anxiety,
fear, envy, resentment, pride, recollection, death, intoxication, sleep, awakening,
shame, epilepsy, delusion, equanimity, lassitude, agitation, deliberation, and dissimulation.
Disease, insanity, the result of past actions, longing, and fickleness—these thirty and these three [make thirty-three].
Disgust (*nirveda*) is self-contempt arising from envy and other such emotions toward those who have attained knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
In that state, there are anxiety, tears, sighs, change of complexion, labored breathing, and dejection. (Dharmasaṃgraha 4.8)

In this world, exhaustion caused by the fatigue of passion and so forth, as well as thirst and hunger, consists of a loss of vitality, discoloration, trembling, lack of enthusiasm, and feebleness of limb and speech. (Dharmasamuccaya 4.9)
Suspicion that something is meaningless arises from the cruelty of another or from one's own poor conduct;
in this context, trembling, emaciation, staring, and so forth, as well as changes in complexion and voice [are the signs].

Fatigue is the exhaustion resulting from ritual sacrifice and the like; perspiration occurs in this state through massage and similar activities; contentment arises from the power of knowledge and so forth; and fortitude produces undisturbed enjoyment. (Dharmapada-daśottara 4.11)

Lack of comprehension would be dullness [caused] by seeing or hearing what is desired or undesired; in that state, there would be such things as staring with unblinking eyes and remaining silent. (Dharmapada 4.12)
Joy (harṣa) arising from festivals and the like is characterized by cheerfulness, tears, perspiration, and a faltering voice;
dejection (dainya), caused by poverty and similar conditions, is a lack of spirit accompanied by a dark complexion, emaciation, and so forth. (Dharmabindu 4.13)
Fury and ferocity arise from malice, transgression, perversity, and cruelty;
in that state, there are perspiration, shaking of the head, threats, blows, and so forth. (Dharmapada 4.14)
Meditation brings about the attainment of what is desired through reflection; it produces the relief of emptiness and the removal of distress.
From thunder and the like, there arises agitation of the mind, terror, trembling, and so forth.
Envy is the intolerance of another's excellence, born of pride, wickedness, and resentment;
it consists of speaking of faults, contempt, frowning, indignation, anger, and the display of such gestures. (Dharmasaṃgraha 4.16)
Intolerance toward insults, contempt, and the like is stubborn attachment;
its manifestations include weariness, shaking the head, threatening, striking, and so forth. (Dharmapada 4.17)
Pride (*garva*) is intoxication (*mada*) arising from one's lineage, beauty, strength, sovereignty, and so forth;
its actions include insolence, contempt, and looking at others with playful gestures of the limbs. (Dharmasaṃgraha 4.18)
In this context, memory arises from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by similar cognitions, reflections, and so forth;
and when an object appears as something already known, there occur such signs as the raising of the eyebrows.
Death is not mentioned here because it is well-known and because it is undesirable.

Excessive joy from drinking is intoxication (*mada*), characterized by faltering limbs, speech, and gait; here, sleep, laughter, and weeping occur among those who are superior, middling, and inferior respectively. Sleep arises from that [intoxication], wherein the activity of inhalation and exhalation is paramount. (Dharmasaṃgraha 4.20)
Sleep is the closing of the mind caused by anxiety, laziness, fatigue, and so forth;

in that state, there occur yawning, stretching of the limbs, closing of the eyes, somnolence, and the like. Awakening results from digestion and other factors; in that [process], there is yawning and rubbing of the eyes. (Dharmasamuccaya 4.21)
Shame, characterized by the absence of audacity due to misconduct and the like, may be inferred from such signs as turning away the limbs, pallor of the face, and looking downward. (Dharmakośa 4.22)
Possession by spirits, suffering from planetary influences, and epilepsy occur according to their respective rules;
[the symptoms include] trembling of the earth, shaking, perspiration, salivation, the emission of foam, and so forth. (Dharmapada-daśottara 4.23)
Delusion is a state of mental confusion caused by fear, the onset of suffering, and brooding;
therein are found ignorance, wandering, striking, reeling, and the like. (Dharmapada 4.24)
Through the instruction on cutting through delusion and by means of the treatises and so forth, the intellect attains the realization of reality;
one should abandon laziness, which is characterized by yawning, smiling, and so on, born of weariness and sloth. (Dharmapada-daśaka 4.25)

In this [drama], there is agitation arising from battle, the employment of weapons and elephants caused by the onset of an army, being smeared with dust due to the wind, and swift movement on foot; likewise, when rain falls, the limbs become contracted;
and due to portents, there is a drooping of the limbs, as well as the expressions of grief and joy produced by what is harmful and beneficial.
With mouths clouded by smoke from fire, they dispelled the trembling caused by the pillars made of elephant-hide.
Reasoning (*tarka*) is deliberation; it causes the eyebrows, head, and fingers to dance due to doubt.
*Avahitthā* is the distortion of the limbs for the purpose of concealing transformations such as shame.
Diseases are those arising from the derangement of the humors (*sannipāta*) and so forth; their detailed classification is found elsewhere.
In this state, there is the insanity of acting without foresight, caused by the derangement of the humors (sannipāta), possession by spirits (graha), and so forth;
it is characterized by weeping, singing, laughing, and sitting [motionlessly]. (Dharmasamuccaya 4.28)
Despair (*viṣāda*) is the depletion of the *sattva* quality caused by the failure of an undertaking already begun;
it brings about sighing, heaving, mental anguish, and the seeking of companions. (Dharmapada-daśottara 4.29)
The inability to endure time, longing, and the desire for pleasure arise from delight in beautiful things;
therein [are found] heaving sighs, deep breaths, heartache, perspiration, and agitation.
Restlessness, however, is instability arising from stinginess, hatred, passion, and so forth;
in that state, there occur such things as reviling, harshness, and acting according to one's own whims. (Dharmasaṃgraha 4.31)
Whether by contrary or non-contrary states, it is not interrupted;
like a salt-mine, that stable one draws others into its own nature. DhDaś_4.32.

Love, energy, disgust, anger, laughter, pride, fear, sorrow, and some also say tranquility—these are the [stable] emotions; however, there is no "nourishment" (puṣṭi) for this [tranquility] in dramatic performances.
How could that which is non-abiding—due to its lack of identity with the initial state of detachment and so forth—be savored?
Its cultivation leads only to a loss of flavor; therefore, eight [mental states] are considered to be stable. (DhDaś 4.34)

Just as an action, though not explicitly stated, is understood from the context and other factors and constitutes the meaning of a sentence when joined with its factors of action (*kāraka*s), so too is a stable emotion (*sthāyībhāva*) [understood] through other [emotions].
That alone is the aesthetic flavor (rasa), because it is sweet, because it exists only for the connoisseur (rasika),
because it does not belong to the subject of imitation, and because the poem is not directed toward that [subject].
The perception of the observer involves the occurrence of shame, envy, attachment, and aversion, because it is like the sight of a worldly man united with his own beloved wife. DhDaś_4.37.
Rāma and others serve as the illustrators of the states such as the *dhīrodātta* (noble and self-controlled);
they manifest the *rasas* such as love (*rati*), which then bring aesthetic relish to the connoisseur.
Just as children playing with elephants and other creatures made of clay find pleasure in their own enthusiasm,
so too do the listeners find delight in [the deeds of] Arjuna and others.

The aesthetic relish (*svāda*) arising from the contemplation of the meaning of a poem is not denied to the dancer; yet that relish, due to the merging with the meaning of the poem, does not originate from self-bliss. (DhDaś 4.40)
It is fourfold through expansion, extension, agitation, and distraction,
occurring respectively in the minds [of those experiencing] the erotic, the heroic, the loathsome, and the furious sentiments.
For those very same [factors] are the causes of the excellence of laughter, wonder, fear, and compassion;
therefore, they are produced by them, and for this very reason, there is this restriction.

The excellence of tranquility is inexpressible; yet, through the objects of poetry—such as the moon, despondency, and horripilation—which have attained the status of excitants (*vibhāva*), transitory states (*sañcārin*), and ensuants (*anubhāva*), it takes on the nature of joy and the other [rasas]. (Dharmakīrti’s *Daśanāmaka*, 4.43)
When cultivated, that which remains as a stable state and is relished is proclaimed to be *rasa*.
There is identity of definition because of the identity of the *vibhāvas*, due to the non-difference between *rasa* and *bhāva*.
Rati is that state of delight belonging to a young couple who are mutually enamored, consisting of the enjoyment of beautiful places, arts, times, dress, pleasures,
and so forth; when it is intensely thrilled by sweet physical gestures, that very Rati becomes the Erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).
Those born of the [primary] emotions, the eight stable ones, the thirty-three transitory states, and the three involuntary states—
these indeed constitute the forty-nine mental factors (bhāvas).
When bound by reasoning, they bring [the mind] to full maturity;
laziness, cruelty, death, and disgust—
based upon that [mind], these are held to be contrary to non-duality.

In that regard, non-union (ayoga) occurs even when there is mutual passion between two young people who are of one mind, due to dependence on others, by fate, or because of physical separation. (Dharmasamuccaya 4.47)
That [passion] has ten stages therein; first, longing, then reflection,
remembrance, discourse on virtues, agitation, lamentation, madness, fever, numbness,
and death— each succeeding stage being a more wretched state.
There is a longing for that beloved who is beautiful in every limb;
and upon seeing or hearing of him, there arise wonder, bliss, and trepidation.
He sees her directly in effigies, dreams, reflections, and illusions;
he hears of her through the pretext of a friend’s song or the praise of virtues by bards and panegyrists.
The mental states such as anxiety (*cintā*) and others, along with their attendant powers and determinants, have been previously shown;
the teachers have generally indicated that they consist of ten stages through their common occurrence.
However, in the compositions of great poets, their infinity is observed.

Why does longing not arise from what has been seen or heard? Why does no yearning occur when there is non-attainment? And why does no despondency or exhaustion result from excessive reflection? (Dharmapada 4.52)

Separation (*viprayoga*), which is a state of disunion, is of two kinds based on the distinction between established trust and estrangement; it is further divided by the difference between pride (*māna*) and separation due to travel (*pravāsa*). Pride, moreover, arises from either love or jealousy. (Dharmakīrti’s *Daśarūpaka* 4.53)
In that regard, *māna* (pride) occurs between two lovers who have become estranged due to anger.

Among women, *māna* is caused by jealousy; it is *kopa* (anger) when the beloved is perceived to be attached to another woman—whether this attachment is heard of from the mouth of a friend, inferred, or directly seen. In this context, "hearing" refers to learning of it from a female companion. (Dharmakīrti’s Daśarūpa 4.54)
Inference is seen to be threefold: that based on dreaming, that based on the marks of enjoyment, and that based on slips of the tongue; while direct perception is the domain of the senses.
One should treat him with increasing gravity through six means: conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, bowing, indifference, and by instilling a different sentiment. (Dharmasaṃgraha 4.56)
In that regard, conciliation consists of gentle speech; sowing dissension is the winning over of his friends;
bribery is the offering of ornaments and such under the guise of a gift; and prostration is falling at his feet. (Dharmapada 4.57)
But when passion (*sāma*) and the other [strategies] have been exhausted, there may be disregard through indifference;
and from impetuosity, fear, joy, and so forth, there arises another rasa characterized by the abandonment of anger.
Furthermore, the gestures of anger of women have already been explained previously. (Dharmakīrti’s *Daśagītikā* 4.58)
Separation due to a task, haste, or a curse results in dwelling in different lands;
therein, for both [the lover and the beloved], there is weeping, sighing, emaciation, and disheveled hair.

The second [type] arises suddenly from a divine or human calamity; the third is born of a curse, which causes a change in one's natural form even in the presence [of the original state]. (Dharmapada-daśottara 4.60)
But when one person has died and another laments there, that is merely grief;
because it rests upon two different subjects, it is not *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment), yet once [the other] has recovered, it is not the other [sentiment, *karuṇa*, either].

The woman longing due to separation from her lover, the one whose beloved has gone abroad, the one separated by a quarrel, the one jealous out of suspicion, and the one deceived—these are the types of the *khaṇḍitā*. (Dharmakīrti’s Daśarūpaka 4.62)
When two amorous persons, being mutually favorable, engage in looking at one another, touching, and so forth, that is the enjoyment (saṃbhoga) filled with joy. (Dharmasaṃgraha 4.63)
Therein proceed the ten gestures of women, such as playfulness and the rest,
which are appropriate to their courtesy, gentleness, and love toward the beloved.
The beloved husband should delight her with flattering words, artistic performances, games, and the like;
he should not engage in anything vulgar, nor anything that causes the failure of their amorous play.
A hero is the source of enthusiasm through majesty, discipline, resolve, courage, lack of despondency, propriety, wonder, valor, and so forth;
and he [is further characterized] by the application of compassion, battle, and generosity.
It is said that here, pride of intellect, steadfastness, and exultation are threefold.
The *bībhatsa* (the loathsome) is the sole source of disgust, consisting primarily of worms, putrid odors,

and vomiting; it causes agitation through blood, entrails, bones, fat, flesh, and the like, and is characterized by a pure aversion toward the hips, breasts, and other parts of the body due to world-weariness (*vairāgya*), being encompassed by these manifesting emotions (*anubhāva*).
In this world, agitation, pain, fear, and so forth [are manifested] by means of such things as the contraction of the nose and mouth.
His nourishment consists of anger, envy, enmity, and deformity; his younger brother is Fierce Agitation,
accompanied by gnashing teeth, trembling lips, knitted brows, perspiration, and a flushed face,
along with the exultation toward enemies, boastfulness, the seizing of meat, striking the earth, and the taking of vows.
In this state, there arise indignation, intoxication, forgetfulness, fickleness, envy, excessive impetuosity, and so forth.
Laughter arises from the distorted appearance, speech, or dress of oneself or another; its nourishment is known as the comic sentiment (*hāsya*), which consists of three types of characters.
A smile here is one with eyes blossoming, while a laugh is that in which the teeth are slightly visible;
a chuckle is with a sweet voice, and this, accompanied by a shaking of the head, is a derisive laugh.
A smile with tearful eyes and agitated limbs becomes a loud laugh;
these two types of laughter each occur respectively in the superior, middling, and inferior [categories].
Sleep, laziness, fatigue, exhaustion, and fainting are its concomitants;
the aesthetic flavor of wonder (adbhuta-rasa) consists of a self characterized by amazement through objects that transcend the world. (Dharmakīrti-daśottara 4.72)

The transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas) arising from this [state] consist of praise, tears, trembling, perspiration, and faltering speech; they are characterized primarily by the force of joy and steadfastness.
The *bhayānaka* (terrifying) aesthetic sentiment arises from creatures with distorted voices and forms;
it is characterized by trembling of all limbs, perspiration, emaciation, and loss of composure, along with its congeners such as dejection, agitation, delusion, and terror. (Dharmapada 4.74)
Upon the loss of what is desired and the attainment of what is undesired, the compassionate [feeling] arises, consisting of sorrow;
following that are sighing, gasping, weeping, paralysis, lamentation, and so forth.
Sleep, epilepsy, dejection, illness, death, laziness, agitation,
despondency, stupor, madness, anxiety, and so forth are the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*).

States such as affection and devotion, and tastes such as hunting and gambling, are not mentioned separately because they are clearly included within [the categories of] joy, enthusiasm, and so forth. (Dharmapada-daśottara 4.77)
The thirty-six ornaments and so forth, the twenty-one means such as conciliation (sāma),
and the subsidiary elements of the junctures and intervals— these exist within those [dramas] along with their poetic ornaments.
Whether it be a charming or loathsome object, noble or base, fierce, serene, profound, or deformed—
whether it be a real thing or even a non-entity, when it is being contemplated by the creative imagination of a poet;
There is nothing in the world that does not attain the state of being a flavor.
By Dhananjaya, the son of Viṣṇu,
this cause of delight for the minds of the learned has been revealed as a discourse for the assembly of the lords of Muñja.
This ten-fold form [of drama] belongs to those possessing ingenuity.
